blocks.content: The trace you just read is a healthy request that ran the whole pipeline. But not every useful trace is a big waterfall. Here's what a failed request looks like, and why its shape alone tells you something.
This is another ready-made TraceQL query, this time for requests that ended in an error. Run it and open one result, the same way as before.
Run the query for failed requests. It opens Explore and returns any error traces from the last hour.
Open one of the error traces by clicking its trace ID.
**If the list is empty, that's expected.** These errors come in bursts, so a quiet minute can return nothing. Widen the time range or run the query again shortly and one will appear.

Notice how different it looks. A successful order runs the whole pipeline: dozens of spans, the deep `recommendations → catalog → SELECT` fan-out. A failed one is short: it short-circuits early, stopping at the step that failed, so it never reaches the rest of the pipeline. The shape alone tells you it stopped early, before you read a single attribute.

This is also where you meet **status codes** (a healthy request returns a success code, a failed one an error code) and the **Errors** filter chip that finds them. The lesson: useful traces aren't always big waterfalls. A small, short trace can tell you exactly where a request gave up.
